title: How a market kills itself
hook: A used-car market can destroy itself, just because buyers can't tell good cars from bad.
caption: A market can kill itself. In a simulated used-car market of {cars} cars where buyers pay only the average, the price fell from {first_price} to {last_price} and just {left} cars were left (Akerlof 1970).

scenes.say: A used-car market can destroy itself, just because buyers can't tell good cars from bad.
Adverse selection: sellers know quality, buyers don't, and good products get pushed out.
Code simulates {cars} cars of random quality. Buyers only pay the average, so good-car owners leave. Repeat.
scenes.note: Simulation: quality uniform 0–100, buyers pay the average

scenes.say: The price starts at {first_price}. After {rounds} rounds it's {last_price}.
Only {left} cars are left on the lot.
Akerlof called it the market for lemons. Without trusted information, markets can vanish.

takeaway: Without trusted information, markets can vanish. Inspections, warranties and honest reviews keep them alive.
